findings.text: KDB release path first attempts to leave the unsafe section and returns early on failure, otherwise releases console ownership and then atomically flushes records queued while that single console was blocked, up to the current reserve sequence.

Cooperative handover first rejects panic on another CPU, same-CPU ownership, permanently unsafe state, and zero wait budget, then publishes a request carrying caller priority. It polls for ownership with a bounded microsecond loop that re-reads state, and on timeout or abort carefully clears only its own request unless a higher priority waiter has superseded it.

Acquisition as the registered waiter requires no panic elsewhere, that the stored request still identifies this priority, and that no owner remains. It then atomically installs caller priority and CPU, clears the request, and carries forward any takeover-induced unsafe marking.

Hostile seizure is permitted only when the context allows unsafe takeover and runs at panic priority. It repeatedly exchanges state to become owner while merging prior unsafe and takeover markers, so the resulting state records that an unsafe interruption occurred.

Ownership is recognized only when both priority and CPU match the caller. That check alone is sufficient with migration, preemption and interrupts excluded; when scheduling or interrupts are possible the caller must additionally hold the driver specific lock that prevents migration, otherwise a same-CPU same-priority reuse can be mistaken for continued ownership.

An owner with no waiter may continue, as may an owner inside an unsafe region even with waiters pending, deferring transfer until the unsafe exit. An owner at a safe point with a higher-priority waiter must release immediately and report loss; the outer caller decides whether to reacquire before proceeding.

Release clears the priority field only while the caller is still the recorded owner, preserves a permanent unsafe indication when a takeover was recorded, and detaches the caller buffer pointer unconditionally.
Entering and leaving the unsafe section are thin toggles around a shared helper that marks the current context safe or unsafe.

Atomic pending flush uses default priority and a two millisecond spin budget. While the console sequence lags the stop point it disables interrupts during acquire, single-record emit, and release. It distinguishes permission failure, loss or transfer of ownership requiring retry, clean exhaustion of backlog, and reserved-but-unfinalized records.

Single-record emit validates that the console is non-blocking with the needed write callback, fetches the next message inside an unsafe section, merges console and record dropped counts, detects replay by comparing the previous-owner sequence, then leaves unsafe before invoking the atomic or threaded driver. Zero-length records only advance accounting. Driver-signalled reacquisition and later ownership loss are both treated as failure. Sequence and dropped updates happen under a second unsafe section.

Console sequence publication attempts a compare exchange on a truncated sequence word; success advances the caller sequence, failure refreshes the caller sequence from the console. The truncation has two build variants, identity and narrowing to 32 bits.

A waiting request is identified solely by equality between stored request priority and expected priority. This works because only a strictly higher priority can wait or steal a request, the priority set is tiny, only one CPU may use panic priority, and lower priorities are disregarded while panic on another CPU is active.

Dropped counts from console and record are summed and surfaced as a banner for classic formatting. If the fetched sequence equals the previous-owner sequence a replay banner is added; otherwise the previous-owner sequence is refreshed by compare exchange only after re-verifying continued ownership.

A formatted message carries sequence, gap count, output length, buffer set, and execution identity. Prepending formats into a scratch area, refuses absurdly large prefixes, truncates the existing output while keeping termination when space is short, then shifts existing bytes forward and inserts the new prefix.

Next-message lookup reads the ring at the requested sequence into scratch for extended mode or directly into output otherwise, derives sequence and missed-record gap, loads execution identity, skips non-forced records above the console loglevel when suppression is allowed, and formats either extended header plus body or classic text.

Extended headers encode combined facility and level, sequence, microsecond timestamp, continuation marker, and optional caller identity. Bodies escape control, high-bit and backslash bytes as hex sequences and append subsystem and device dictionary lines only when values are present, with all appends bounded by remaining space.
A record is suppressed when its level reaches the console loglevel unless a global ignore-loglevel override is active.

Once an unsafe hostile takeover is recorded the console remains unsafe across release and future handover attempts fail; concurrent dropped-counter updates during such takeover are intentionally racy.

Waiting is forbidden for non-panic CPUs while panic executes elsewhere, handover to the same CPU is rejected, and callers with no spin budget cannot request handover. Violations of expected priority ordering and releasing from an unsafe region trigger one-time warnings.
Dropped-count and replay notices share one prepend formatter that inserts a fixed human-readable banner line ahead of the record text.
Loading execution identity into the driver write context has two builds: one copies CPU, process id and command name with a compile-time size check, the other discards the information.
